pos: n. (Francisco Suárez, 1548–1617, Spanish Jesuit, called Doctor Eximius, author of the Metaphysical Disputations and De Legibus, the most influential Roman philosopher after Aquinas)
etymology: Spanish Suárez, a patronymic from Suero; Francisco, from Latin Franciscus, the Frank.
biblical_def: Francisco Suárez reorganized scholastic philosophy. His Disputationes Metaphysicae of 1597 was the first metaphysics in the West arranged as a system in its own right rather than as a commentary on Aristotle, and it was read in Protestant universities for a century — the Reformed scholastics learned much of their vocabulary of essence, modes and causes from a Jesuit. His De Legibus is the greater book for the history of law. It distinguishes eternal, natural, divine positive and human law; grounds natural law in the rational nature God created rather than in bare divine fiat; derives civil authority from God through the community, so that no king holds power immediately from heaven; and concludes that a tyrant may in extremity be resisted. Rom 2:15 is the foundation he builds on — men “shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness” — and Jas 4:12 the limit, “There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy.” Isa 33:22 says it of the LORD: “the LORD is our lawgiver.” He also taught congruism, a softened Molinism, on grace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the law of nature as that law which God has prescribed to his rational creatures, and which is discoverable by the light of reason or revelation.
webster_full: LAW, n. A rule, particularly an established or permanent rule, prescribed by the supreme power of a state to its subjects.
The law of nature, is a rule of conduct arising out of the natural relations of human beings established by the Creator, and existing prior to any positive precept.
The moral law is summarily contained in the decalogue, written by the finger of God on two tables of stone.
scriptures: Rom 2:15
Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;)
Jas 4:12
There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?
For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us.
Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
corruption_summary: Suarez grounded natural law so firmly in created reason that his successors learned to discuss it without reference to the Lawgiver.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed tradition affirms natural law: Rom 2:15 says the work of the law is written in the heart of the pagan, and the 1689 Confession assumes a moral order binding all men. Suárez states this better than most. The difficulty is a matter of weight. By locating the obligation so completely in the rationality of created nature, he made it possible for the next two centuries to treat natural law as a free-standing science — Grotius would say it would hold even if God did not exist — and from there the road runs to a secular rights theory with no Lawgiver in it. Jas 4:12 is the sentence that keeps the doctrine Christian: there is one lawgiver.

The second corruption is the use made of his political conclusions in his own church. Suárez derived civil power from God through the community, which is sound against the divine right of kings; he also defended an indirect papal power to depose rulers, which hands the sword back to the church by another door. Scripture gives the magistrate his office and gives the church none of it. The recovery is natural law confessed with its Author named, the magistrate honoured in his own sphere, and no bishop empowered to unmake a king: “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7), which no natural light can do.
roots_summary: Greek nomos (G3551), law; nomothetes (G3550), a lawgiver; Hebrew chaqaq (H2710), to inscribe, to decree.
roots_lines: Greek nomos (G3551) — law; Romans 2:15.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience, co-knowledge; Romans 2:15.
Greek nomothetes (G3550) — a lawgiver; James 4:12.
Hebrew chaqaq (H2710) — to inscribe, to decree, hence lawgiver; Isaiah 33:22.
Hebrew tamim (H8549) — perfect, complete; Psalm 19:7.
usage: “the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom 2:15) — the foundation he built on.
“There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy” (Jas 4:12) — the limit his successors forgot.
“The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7) — what natural light cannot do.

pos: n. (Domingo Báñez, 1528–1604, Spanish Dominican Thomist, confessor to Teresa of Ávila and chief opponent of Molina in the controversy de auxiliis over grace and free will)
etymology: Spanish Báñez, a family name of Valladolid; Domingo, of the Lord's day, the name of his order's founder.
biblical_def: Domingo Báñez held the chief chair at Salamanca and is the nearest Rome ever came to a predestinarian theology. Against the Jesuit Molina, who taught that God foreknows by middle knowledge what each free creature would do under any circumstance and elects accordingly, Báñez taught praemotio physica: God moves the will efficaciously from within, so that the creature acts freely and yet infallibly does what God has determined, and grace is efficacious of itself and not by the will's consent. The dispute went to Rome, where a special congregation sat for ten years and issued no decision — both opinions were left standing, which is itself the verdict Rome gave. Báñez's texts are the Reformed ones. Eph 1:5 has God “Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will”; Rom 9:18, “whom he will he hardeneth”; and Joh 6:44, “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.” Pro 16:9 holds both halves: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines predestination as the act of decreeing or foreordaining events; the decree of God by which he hath, for his own glory, foreordained whatever comes to pass.
webster_full: PREDESTINA'TION, n. The act of decreeing or foreordaining events; the decree of God by which he hath, for his own glory, foreordained whatever comes to pass.
PREDES'TINATE, v.t. To predetermine or foreordain; to appoint or ordain beforehand by an unchangeable purpose.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favour of God.
scriptures: Eph 1:5
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
Rom 9:18
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
corruption_summary: Rome heard the Thomist case for efficacious grace argued for ten years and declined to decide, which is how a church keeps a doctrine it cannot deny and will not confess.
corruption_paragraphs: The de auxiliis congregation is one of the most revealing episodes in Roman history. Báñez argued from Scripture and Aquinas that grace is efficacious intrinsically and that God's decree is not conditioned on foreseen choices; Molina argued that it is. Rome permitted both and silenced neither, so that a communion which anathematized the Reformed doctrine at Trent went on housing a school that taught much of it. The permanent lesson is that an institution which makes its own authority the rule can tolerate contradictory answers, because the question of what Scripture says has ceased to be decisive. Rom 9:18 is not ambiguous.

A Reformed reader should also mark where Báñez is not with us. He held physical premotion within a Tridentine framework of infused justification increased by merit, so his predestinarianism does not issue in sola fide, and he was Teresa's confessor in a thoroughly Roman piety. The agreement is real and partial. Joh 6:44 states the monergism both he and the Reformed confess — no man can come unless drawn — and the Reformation's further step was to see that the drawing terminates in a righteousness imputed, not infused.
roots_summary: Greek proorizo (G4309), to predestinate; skleruno (G4645), to harden; helko (G1670), to draw.
roots_lines: Greek proorizo (G4309) — to mark out beforehand, to predestinate; Ephesians 1:5.
Greek eudokia (G2107) — good pleasure; Ephesians 1:5.
Greek skleruno (G4645) — to harden; Romans 9:18.
Greek helko (G1670) — to draw, to drag; John 6:44.
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to establish, to direct; Proverbs 16:9.
usage: “Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children” (Eph 1:5) — the decree he defended.
“whom he will he hardeneth” (Rom 9:18) — the clause Molina had to soften.
“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44) — monergism from the Lord's mouth.

pos: n. (Caspar Cruciger the Elder, 1504–1548, professor at Wittenberg, Melanchthon's closest colleague and the editor who preserved much of Luther's preaching and lecturing)
etymology: Latinized from German Kreuziger, cross-bearer; Caspar, from the traditional name of a magus.
biblical_def: Caspar Cruciger is the kind of man a movement cannot do without and historians forget. A superb stenographer and a careful editor, he took down Luther's lectures and sermons, prepared them for the press, and edited large parts of the Wittenberg edition of his works; Luther said Cruciger alone could read his hand and his mind together. He taught theology and Hebrew, served as rector, took part in the colloquies at Marburg, Worms and Regensburg, and was trusted by both Luther and Melanchthon in a faculty where that was becoming rare. He died at forty-four, worn out. His office is the one Paul commits in 2Ti 2:2: “the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.” Psa 145:4 names the chain — “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” — and Act 20:27 the standard for an editor as for a preacher: “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an editor as one who revises, corrects and prepares a book or paper for publication; and to transmit as to send from one person or place to another.
webster_full: ED'ITOR, n. A publisher; particularly, a person who superintends an impression of a book; one who revises, corrects and prepares a book for publication.
TRANSMIT', v.t. To send from one person or place to another; to cause to pass to another place.
2. To suffer to pass through; as, glass transmits light.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
corruption_summary: A reformation is carried by its stenographers as truly as by its prophets, and a movement that honours only its founders will lose its texts.
corruption_paragraphs: Luther preached and lectured far more than he wrote out, and most of what survives survives because men like Cruciger were in the room with a pen. The transmission of doctrine is not a lesser calling than its discovery: 2Ti 2:2 makes the commitment of the deposit to faithful men a direct apostolic charge, and the chain it describes has four links — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others also. A church that prizes only the originator undervalues exactly the work that puts the original in its own hands.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, and the principle to recover is the duty of faithful transmission, with its attendant honesty. An editor shapes what he transmits; the Wittenberg editors sometimes smoothed Luther, and the nineteenth-century critical editions had to undo it. Act 20:27 binds the editor as much as the preacher — the whole counsel, not the convenient part — and Pro 25:11 describes what careful work produces: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.”
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit, to entrust; paradidomi (G3860), to deliver over; Hebrew nagad (H5046), to declare.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to set before, to commit in trust; 2 Timothy 2:2.
Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy; 2 Timothy 2:2.
Hebrew shabach (H7623) — to praise, to commend; Psalm 145:4.
Greek hupostellomai (G5288) — to withhold, to shun declaring; Acts 20:27.
Greek boule (G1012) — counsel, purpose; Acts 20:27.
usage: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — his office exactly.
“One generation shall praise thy works to another” (Psa 145:4) — the chain he served.
“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — the editor's standard too.

pos: n. (Justus Jonas, 1493–1555, Wittenberg theologian and translator, Luther's companion to Worms and at his deathbed, who preached his funeral sermon)
etymology: Latinized from Jodocus Koch; he took the names Justus, just, and Jonas — the latter the Authorized Version's own spelling of Jonah.
biblical_def: Justus Jonas was a lawyer and humanist converted by Luther's writings, who gave up a canonry to come to Wittenberg and remained the movement's most useful companion. He rode with Luther to the Diet of Worms in 1521 and stood by him there; he translated Luther's and Melanchthon's Latin works into German and his German into Latin, so that each reached the audience the other could not; he organized the churches of Saxony and Halle; he was present at Eisleben when Luther died in 1546 and preached the funeral sermon. Friendship of this order is a scriptural category, not a sentimental one. Pro 17:17 says “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity”; Ecc 4:9, “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.” Php 2:22 describes what Timothy was to Paul and Jonas to Luther: “as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel.” 2Ti 4:11 is the other side, the loneliness when such men are gone: “Only Luke is with me.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a friend as one who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection.
webster_full: FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company, and to seek to promote his happiness and prosperity.
2. One not hostile; as, he is no friend to our cause.
3. An attendant; a companion.
scriptures: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Php 2:22
But ye know the proof of him, that, as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.
corruption_summary: Jonas is the proof that the Reformation was carried by companies of men, not by a solitary genius, which is the shape the hero-histories lose.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular accounts of the Reformation run on single figures: Luther at Worms, Calvin in Geneva, Knox before the queen. The documents show something different — Luther with Jonas and Melanchthon and Bugenhagen and Cruciger, translating each other, covering each other's absences, correcting each other's excesses. Ecc 4:9 is the plain arithmetic of it, and Php 2:22 names the relation that actually transmits a ministry. A church that tells its history as a procession of great men teaches its people to wait for one, instead of building the companies that do the work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the ordinary labour of the second man. Jonas translated for thirty years so that Germans could read Melanchthon and Latin Europe could read Luther, and no doctrine bears his name. 2Ti 4:11 is worth setting beside it: the apostle at the end writes “Only Luke is with me,” and the sentence is both a measure of how much such companions are worth and a warning of how a man feels when they are gone. Pro 17:17 makes the friend's constancy a matter of righteousness, not temperament.
roots_summary: Hebrew rea (H7453), a friend, a companion; Greek douleuo (G1398), to serve; euchrestos (G2173), profitable.
roots_lines: Hebrew rea (H7453) — a friend, a neighbour; Proverbs 17:17.
Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — adversity, distress; Proverbs 17:17.
Hebrew sakar (H7939) — reward, wages; Ecclesiastes 4:9.
Greek douleuo (G1398) — to serve as a bondman; Philippians 2:22.
Greek euchrestos (G2173) — useful, profitable; 2 Timothy 4:11.
usage: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17) — Worms and Eisleben both.
“Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9) — the arithmetic of the Reformation.
“as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel” (Php 2:22) — what he was to Luther.

pos: n. (Georg Spalatin, 1484–1545, secretary and chaplain to Frederick the Wise, the courtier through whom Luther was protected and the Elector persuaded)
etymology: Latinized from Burkhardt of Spalt in Franconia — Spalatinus, of Spalt; Georg, from Greek georgos, a husbandman.
biblical_def: Georg Spalatin never wrote a book of doctrine and is one of the three or four men without whom there would have been no Reformation. As private secretary, chaplain and librarian to Frederick the Wise of Saxony, he had the ear of the one prince able to shield Luther from the empire, and he used it continuously for twenty years: translating Luther's Latin for the Elector, interpreting the Elector's mind to Luther, drafting the refusal to surrender him after Exsurge Domine, and arranging the kidnapping that hid him in the Wartburg after Worms. He was cautious where Luther was bold and often restrained him, sometimes rightly. His office is Nehemiah's. “Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven” (Neh 2:4) is the courtier's moment, and Neh 1:11 the prayer before it: “grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” Dan 1:9 names who gives such favour: “Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs.” Pro 16:7 is the providence of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines favor as kind regard; kindness; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition; and a courtier as one who attends or frequents the courts of princes.
webster_full: FA'VOR, n. Kind regard; kindness; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition.
2. Support; defense; vindication; or disposition to aid, befriend, support, promote or justify.
COUR'TIER, n. One who attends or frequents the courts of princes.
scriptures: Neh 2:4
Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven.
Neh 1:11

O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king's cupbearer.
Dan 1:9
Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs.
Pro 16:7
When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.
corruption_summary: God protected the Reformation through a civil servant, and a church that only recognizes pulpit callings cannot see what He was doing.
corruption_paragraphs: Spalatin held no office in the church and spent his working life drafting letters for a prince, and the gospel in Germany survived because he was where he was. Scripture is full of the pattern — Joseph in the prison and then the palace, Daniel with the prince of the eunuchs, Nehemiah with the cup, Esther with access, Erastus the chamberlain — and in every case the favour is traced to God, not to the courtier's skill. Dan 1:9 is explicit about the agent. A doctrine of vocation that ranks the secretary beneath the preacher has not read these accounts carefully.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the lawful use of access, together with its limit. Spalatin's caution more than once nearly smothered the thing he was protecting, and he advised Luther to be quiet at moments when silence would have been surrender; the courtier's temptation is to make prudence the highest virtue. Neh 2:4 holds the balance exactly — the request is made to the king, and it is made by a man who prayed first to the God of heaven, which is what keeps access from becoming mere management.
roots_summary: Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy, lovingkindness; racham (H7356), tender love; ratsah (H7521), to be pleased with.
roots_lines: Hebrew baqqashah (H1246) — a request, a petition; Nehemiah 2:4.
Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — mercies, tender love; Nehemiah 1:11, Daniel 1:9.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, steadfast love; Daniel 1:9.
Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to accept; Proverbs 16:7.
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to be at peace; Proverbs 16:7.
usage: “So I prayed to the God of heaven” (Neh 2:4) — the courtier's moment.
“grant him mercy in the sight of this man” (Neh 1:11) — the prayer behind the access.
“God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs” (Dan 1:9) — who gives such favour.

pos: n. (Veit Dietrich, 1506–1549, preacher of St Sebald's in Nuremberg, Luther's amanuensis at the Coburg during the Diet of Augsburg and the editor of his house-postils)
etymology: German Veit, from Latin Vitus; Dietrich, from Theodoric, ruler of the people. Latinized Vitus Theodorus.
biblical_def: Veit Dietrich lived in Luther's house as a student, became his secretary, and was the companion who stayed with him at the Coburg fortress through the summer of 1530 while the Augsburg Confession was presented without him — writing letters, taking dictation, and watching a man under great strain. He went home to Nuremberg, became preacher at St Sebald's, and spent the rest of his life putting Luther into the hands of ordinary households: the Hauspostille, the children's questions, the prayer-books, the agenda for the Nuremberg churches. The calling is the one Job wished for — “Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!” (Job 19:23) — and the office is Baruch's in Jer 36:4, who “wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD.” Rom 16:22 shows that the New Testament itself was written by such men: “I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord.” Pro 25:11 is the craft he practised on another man's preaching.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an amanuensis as a person who writes what another dictates; and a postil as a marginal note; a short comment or exposition on a text.
webster_full: AMANUEN'SIS, n. A person whose employment is to write what another dictates.
POS'TIL, n. A marginal note; a short comment or exposition.
POS'TIL, v.t. To write marginal notes; to gloss; to illustrate with marginal notes.
scriptures: Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!
Jer 36:4
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book.
I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
corruption_summary: The household sermon-book is the forgotten engine of the Reformation, and its editors are the forgotten men.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformation reached ordinary Germans less through the great treatises than through postils, catechisms and prayer-books read aloud in kitchens, and Dietrich made more of those than almost anyone. It is worth noticing what the office involves: Jer 36:4 shows Baruch writing from the prophet's mouth, and Rom 16:22 shows Tertius writing an inspired epistle at Paul's dictation — the amanuensis is inside the biblical record, not a footnote to it. A movement reaches a household through somebody who prepared a book for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is family worship with substantial material in it. The house-postil assumed that a father would read a serious exposition to his household weekly, and that the children would be questioned on it. Where that practice died, the next generation was catechized by whatever else was at hand. Job 19:23 is a wish God granted abundantly, and the right response to having the words printed in a book is to read them at the table.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write; megillah (H4039), a roll, a scroll; Greek grapho (G1125), to write.
roots_lines: Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, to inscribe; Job 19:23, Jeremiah 36:4.
Hebrew chaqaq (H2710) — to cut in, to engrave, printed in a book; Job 19:23.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, a written scroll; Jeremiah 36:4.
Greek grapho (G1125) — to write; Romans 16:22.
Hebrew ophen (H655) — a fit season, fitly; Proverbs 25:11.
usage: “Oh that my words were now written!” (Job 19:23) — the wish his press answered.
“Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD” (Jer 36:4) — the amanuensis in Scripture.
“I Tertius, who wrote this epistle” (Rom 16:22) — the office inside the canon.

pos: n. (Erasmus Sarcerius, 1501–1559, Lutheran superintendent in Nassau and at Eisleben, whose visitation articles and pastoral manuals gave the German churches their working order and discipline)
etymology: Latinized from German Sarcer; he took Erasmus as a humanist given name. Not Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.
biblical_def: Erasmus Sarcerius did the unglamorous work that decides whether a reformation survives its first generation. As superintendent he visited parishes, examined ministers, catalogued what he found, and wrote it up: handbooks of pastoral theology, a book on the office and duties of a minister, articles for church visitation, and treatises on marriage and on discipline. He fought for the right of the church to excommunicate without the magistrate's leave — a real battle in Lutheran territories, where the prince commonly held that power — and he convened synods at Eisleben to put discipline in the hands of the ministry. His charter is Tit 1:5: Titus is left in Crete “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city.” Act 14:23 records the practice, that “they had ordained them elders in every church.” 1Ti 5:17 honours “the elders that rule well,” and Heb 13:17 charges the flock to obey those who “watch for your souls, as they that must give account.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discipline, in a church sense, as the execution of the laws by which the church is governed, and the infliction of the penalties enjoined against offenders.
webster_full: DIS'CIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; cultivation and improvement, comprehending instruction in arts, sciences, correct sentiments, morals and manners.
4. In a church sense, the execution of the laws by which the church is governed, and the infliction of the penalties enjoined against offenders, who profess the religion of Jesus Christ.
VISITA'TION, n. The act of visiting; the object of visitation; also, the act of a superior who visits his inferiors.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: Sarcerius fought to keep church discipline out of the prince's hands, and where that fight was lost the Lutheran churches became departments of state.
corruption_paragraphs: The German settlement handed the oversight of the churches to the territorial prince, and the consistories he appointed came to hold the keys. Sarcerius saw what it would cost and spent his last years contending that excommunication belongs to the ministry because Christ gave it there. He largely lost, and the consequence is the state-church Lutheranism of the next three centuries, in which a minister could be installed, moved or silenced by a civil authority. Heb 13:17 assumes officers who “must give account” to God for souls, which is not an account a government department can render.

The second corruption is the opposite modern failure: no discipline at all. Where the Reformation's heirs grew wary of consistories they often abandoned the practice entirely, and a church that will not exercise the discipline Christ commanded cannot keep its membership honest or its table holy. Tit 1:5 and Act 14:23 make an ordered eldership in every congregation the apostolic norm, and discipline exercised by those elders — patient, graduated, aimed at restoration — is a mark of the true church, not an embarrassment in its history.
roots_summary: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930), to set further in order; cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint, to ordain; agrupneo (G69), to watch.
roots_lines: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930) — to set in order what remains; Titus 1:5.
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — an elder; Titus 1:5, 1 Timothy 5:17.
Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint, to ordain; Acts 14:23.
Greek proistemi (G4291) — to rule, to preside; 1 Timothy 5:17.
Greek agrupneo (G69) — to be sleepless, to watch; Hebrews 13:17.
usage: “set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — his charter.
“they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the apostolic practice.
“they watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17) — an account no department renders.

pos: n. (Jakob Andreae, 1528–1590, chancellor of Tübingen and chief architect of the Formula of Concord, which ended thirty years of war within Lutheranism)
etymology: German Andreae, a Latinized patronymic from Andreas; Jakob, from Hebrew Yaaqob, Jacob.
biblical_def: Jakob Andreae inherited a wreck. After Luther's death the Lutheran churches tore themselves apart in a series of controversies — over whether good works are necessary to salvation, over free will, over whether indifferent things may be conceded to the emperor, over original sin, over the Supper — with Melanchthon's party and the strict Lutherans anathematizing each other. Andreae travelled, negotiated, drafted and redrafted for more than a decade, and with Martin Chemnitz and David Chytraeus produced the Formula of Concord of 1577, subscribed by some eight thousand ministers and most Lutheran territories. It is a genuine achievement of churchmanship. The texts he worked by are Eph 4:3, “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace,” and 1Co 1:10, “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you.” Rom 15:5 asks God to “grant you to be likeminded one toward another according to Christ Jesus” — the qualifying clause that keeps unity from becoming mere agreement. He was no friend to the Reformed and hardened the Lutheran position against them on the Supper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concord as agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests; and a formula as a prescribed form; a rule or model.
webster_full: CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests; peace; harmony.
FORM'ULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model.
2. In church affairs, a confession of faith; as the formula of concord.
scriptures: Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Rom 15:5
Now the God of patience and consolation grant you to be likeminded one toward another according to Christ Jesus:
Php 2:2
Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind.
corruption_summary: Andreae proved that real concord is reached by settling the doctrine, not by agreeing to leave it unsettled.
corruption_paragraphs: The Formula of Concord is instructive because of how it worked. It did not paper over the controversies; it took each one, stated the error on both sides, and defined the position, at length. That is why it held. The contrast with Regensburg and Florence is exact: a union produced by ambiguity collapses, and a concord produced by definition endures. 1Co 1:10 asks for one speech and one judgment, and Rom 15:5 specifies the standard of likemindedness — “according to Christ Jesus” — which rules out a peace reached by lowering it.

The Reformed reader must also note where the Formula was used against him. Its articles on the Supper and the person of Christ were framed to exclude the Reformed doctrine, asserting a bodily ubiquity of Christ's human nature in order to defend a real bodily presence in the bread. That is the error the Reformed have always identified: a communication of divine attributes to the human nature which Chalcedon's “without confusion” forbids. Concord within a confession is good; this one was purchased partly by hardening a division that need not have been made, and Php 2:2 is addressed to the whole church of Christ.

roots_lines: Greek henotes (G1775) — oneness, unity; Ephesians 4:3.

“that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — unity by definition, not by silence.
“to be likeminded one toward another according to Christ Jesus” (Rom 15:5) — the qualifying standard.

pos: n. (David Chytraeus, 1530–1600, professor at Rostock, co-author of the Formula of Concord and organizer of the Lutheran churches of Austria and Styria)
etymology: Latinized from German Kochhafe by way of Greek chytra, a cooking pot; David, Hebrew Dawid, beloved.
biblical_def: David Chytraeus studied under Melanchthon at twelve and taught at Rostock for nearly fifty years. He wrote the first Lutheran history of the Augsburg Confession, lectured on nearly the whole of Scripture, and with Andreae and Chemnitz drafted the Formula of Concord — the article on the Lord's Supper and much of the Epitome are largely his. He also did the field work: he was summoned to Austria and Styria to organize churches, draft their orders and examine their ministers, and he travelled to do the same in Saxony and Brandenburg, keeping a careful record of the state of each. The shape of that calling is Act 15:36, where Paul proposes to “go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.” Pro 27:23 is the shepherd's version: “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.” 1Pe 5:2 gives the manner, “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines oversight as superintendence; watchful care; and to visit, in an ecclesiastical sense, as to go to for the purpose of inspection or examination.
webster_full: O'VERSIGHT, n. Superintendence; watchful care; as the oversight of a flock.
2. Omission; neglect; mistake or error which proceeds from inattention.
VIS'IT, v.t. To go or come to see; to attend; as a physician visits his patient. 3. To go to for the purpose of inspection or examination.
scriptures: And some days after Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Eze 34:4

The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them.
corruption_summary: A confession that is written and never visited becomes a paper church, and Chytraeus is the man who went and looked.
corruption_paragraphs: The Formula of Concord would have been a document about doctrine if its authors had not also been the men who rode out to the parishes. Chytraeus did both, and Act 15:36 is the apostolic instinct joining them: having preached the word, go back and see how they do. The temptation in confessional churches is to believe that a well-drafted standard has settled the matter, when the question is always what is actually taught and lived in each congregation. Pro 27:23 makes knowing the state of the flock a duty, not an administrative preference.

The indictment where oversight fails is “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick” (Eze 34:4). The same verse closes with the opposite fault, shepherds who ruled with force and with cruelty, and so names both failures at once — the shepherd who neglects and the shepherd who domineers — and 1Pe 5:2 forbids both, requiring oversight taken willingly and not for gain. The recovery is visitation as a regular part of church order: elders who know their people, and ministers who are examined by brethren who have actually heard them preach.

“Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23) — oversight as duty.

pos: n. (Tilemann Hesshus, 1527–1588, militant Gnesio-Lutheran theologian, expelled in turn from Goslar, Rostock, Heidelberg, Bremen, Magdeburg, Wesel, Jena and Samland for contention)
etymology: German Hesshusen, from the family seat near Wesel; Tilemann, a Low German form of Dietrich or Tilman.
biblical_def: Tilemann Hesshus was learned, courageous and impossible. A strict Lutheran of the Gnesio party, he contended for Luther's doctrine of the Supper against the Reformed, against Melanchthon's followers, against the magistrates who employed him, and against colleagues who largely agreed with him; Calvin wrote a treatise answering him, and Melanchthon's party and his own both found him unmanageable. He was driven from eight posts in thirty years, usually for refusing to submit a disciplinary case to the civil authority or for denouncing a patron from the pulpit. In some of those quarrels he was right, which is what makes him a useful entry rather than merely a sad one. But the ministerial qualifications are not optional: “the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24). Tit 3:9 commands that we “avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain,” and Pro 13:10 names the root: “Only by pride cometh contention.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contention as strife; struggle; a violent effort to obtain something, or to resist a person, claim or injury; and contentious as apt to contend; quarrelsome.
webster_full: CONTEN'TION, n. Strife; struggle; a violent effort to obtain something, or to resist a person, claim or injury; contest; quarrel.
2. Strife in words or debate; quarrel; angry contest; controversy.
CONTEN'TIOUS, a. Apt to contend; quarrelsome; perverse.
scriptures: And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
Tit 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised is wisdom.
Gal 5:15
But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
corruption_summary: Hesshus is the standing warning that a man may be right about the doctrine and disqualified by the manner, and that the manner is also commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to read Hesshus as a figure of fun — eight expulsions — and the serious point is lost. He held positions his own church confessed, he suffered real poverty for refusing to let princes govern the Lord's table, and he was treated badly more than once. And 2Ti 2:24 is part of the same Scripture as the doctrine he defended: the servant of the Lord “must not strive.” Soundness is not a dispensation from gentleness, and the Pastorals list temperament among the qualifications for office precisely because an unquiet man destroys what his doctrine would have built.

The nearer corruption is the modern inversion, which treats any firmness as contentiousness and makes agreeableness the whole of ministerial fitness. Scripture will not have that either: the same apostle who forbids striving commands that gainsayers be convinced, and Hesshus's refusal to surrender discipline to the magistrate was obedience. The distinction Tit 3:9 draws is between strivings that are “unprofitable and vain” and the faith that must be contended for, and Gal 5:15 states the cost of missing it: “if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.”
roots_summary: Greek machomai (G3164), to strive, to quarrel; eris (G2054), strife; Hebrew matsah (H4683), contention.
roots_lines: Greek machomai (G3164) — to fight, to strive; 2 Timothy 2:24.

Hebrew matstsah (H4683) — strife, contention; Proverbs 13:10.

“avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law” (Tit 3:9) — the distinction he lost.
